passages.title: Coral Reefs: Cities Under the Sea
paragraphs: Beneath the warm, clear waters of tropical seas lie some of the busiest places on the planet: coral reefs. They are often called the rainforests of the sea because so many living things make their homes there.

Many people think coral is a rock or a plant, but it is actually an animal! A coral reef is built by tiny creatures called polyps. Each polyp has a soft body and makes a hard, stony skeleton around itself. When millions of polyps live together for hundreds of years, their skeletons pile up and form a reef.

Coral polyps have special partners: tiny algae that live inside their bodies. The algae use sunlight to make food, and they share it with the coral. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe home. The algae also give coral many of its bright colors. This kind of teamwork, where both partners help each other, is called symbiosis.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species depend on them. Fish, sea turtles, sharks, clams and octopuses find food and shelter among the corals. The Philippines is home to Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park, a protected reef in the Sulu Sea that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Sadly, reefs are in danger. When the ocean becomes too warm, corals push out their algae and turn white. This is called coral bleaching. Without their algae, corals can starve. We can help by reducing pollution, protecting sea life and learning more about these underwater cities.

options: The tiny algae living inside it

passages.title: Good Vibrations: How Sound Travels
paragraphs: Clap your hands. Did you hear that? Every sound you have ever heard, from a whisper to a thunderclap, starts the same way: with a vibration. A vibration is a quick back-and-forth movement.

When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes back and forth very fast. The moving string pushes against the air around it and makes the tiny particles of air vibrate too. These particles bump into their neighbors, which bump into their neighbors, passing the vibration along like a wave. This is a sound wave.
When the sound wave reaches you, it enters your ear and makes your eardrum vibrate. Tiny bones inside your ear pass the vibrations along, and your brain turns them into the sounds you recognize.

Sound can travel through air, water and even solid things like wood and metal. In fact, it moves faster through water than through air, and faster still through solids like steel. But sound cannot travel through empty space, because there is no air to carry the vibrations. That is why space is completely silent!

Sound can also bounce. When a sound wave hits a hard surface, like a cliff, and bounces back, you hear an echo. Bats use echoes to find their way in the dark. They make high squeaks and listen for the echoes to learn where things are. This is called echolocation.

passages.title: José Rizal: A Hero Who Loved Learning
paragraphs: José Rizal is one of the national heroes of the Philippines. He was born on June 19, 1861, in the town of Calamba, Laguna. He was the seventh of eleven children in his family.

His first teacher was his mother, Teodora Alonso. She taught him to read when he was very young, and he quickly fell in love with books. As a boy, he also enjoyed drawing, painting and shaping figures out of clay.

Rizal was a brilliant student. He studied at the Ateneo Municipal de Manila and later at the University of Santo Tomas. Then he traveled to Europe to continue his studies. He became an eye doctor and even operated on his own mother's eyes. Rizal could speak many languages and was also a poet, an artist and a scientist.

At that time, the Philippines was ruled by Spain, and many Filipinos were treated unfairly. Rizal used his pen instead of weapons to fight for change. He wrote two famous novels, Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo, which showed the problems in Philippine society and inspired Filipinos to love their country.

The Spanish government saw him as a threat, and he was executed on December 30, 1896. His ideas lived on, however, and helped inspire the fight for freedom. Today, Filipinos remember him every December 30, which is known as Rizal Day.

passages.title: Electricity: From Power Plant to Plug
paragraphs: Flip a switch and the lights come on. Plug in a charger and a phone's battery fills up. But where does that electricity come from, and how does it travel all the way to your home?

Most electricity is made in power plants. Inside many of them is a machine called a generator. When a big coil of wire spins near powerful magnets, electricity starts to flow through the wire. To keep the generator spinning, power plants use steam from burning coal or natural gas, falling water from dams, wind turning giant blades, or heat from deep underground. Solar panels are different: they turn sunlight directly into electricity without spinning anything.

From the power plant, electricity rushes along thick wires held up by tall towers. These are called transmission lines. The electricity travels at a very high voltage so that less of it is wasted over long distances. Before it reaches your neighborhood, machines called transformers lower the voltage to a safer level for homes, schools and stores.

Electricity flows only when it has a complete path, called a circuit. Materials that let electricity pass through easily, like copper and other metals, are called conductors. Materials that block it, like rubber and plastic, are called insulators. That is why electrical wires are made of copper covered in plastic.
Electricity is useful, but it can be very dangerous. Never touch outlets or wires with wet hands, never poke objects into sockets, and stay far away from fallen power lines.

passages.title: Tandang Sora: Mother of the Revolution
paragraphs: Melchora Aquino was born on January 6, 1812, in Banlat, a village in what is now Quezon City. She grew up to be a kind and hardworking woman who ran a small store and farmed rice and sugarcane. People lovingly called her Tandang Sora, meaning Old Sora, because she lived to a very old age.

In 1896, when the Philippine Revolution against Spain began, Tandang Sora was already 84 years old. She was too old to fight, but she found another way to help. She opened her home to members of the Katipunan. She fed hungry revolutionaries, cared for wounded fighters, gave them medicine, and let them hide and hold secret meetings in her home.

Spanish soldiers soon found out. They arrested Tandang Sora and questioned her, but she refused to give away the names or hiding places of the Katipuneros. As punishment, she was sent far from home, into exile on the island of Guam.
After Spain lost control of the Philippines, Tandang Sora returned home in 1903. She lived quietly until she died in 1919, at the age of 107.

Today, Tandang Sora is honored as the Mother of the Philippine Revolution. A major avenue in Quezon City is named after her, and her story reminds Filipinos that everyone, young or old, can serve their country with courage and kindness.

passages.title: Glaciers and Icebergs
paragraphs: In the coldest places on Earth, near the North and South Poles and high in tall mountains, snow falls year after year without ever fully melting. Over hundreds of years, the layers of snow pile up and press down on each other until they turn into thick, solid ice. A huge body of ice like this, heavy enough to move, is called a glacier.

It may be hard to believe, but glaciers flow like very slow rivers. Pulled by their own enormous weight, they creep downhill, sometimes only a few centimeters a day. As they move, they scrape the land beneath them, carving out valleys and carrying rocks for long distances.

When a glacier reaches the sea, big chunks can crack off its front and crash into the water. This is called calving, and the floating chunks are icebergs. Only about one-tenth of an iceberg shows above the water; the other nine-tenths are hidden below the surface. That is why people say something is just "the tip of the iceberg" when there is much more to it than we can see.
Hidden ice can be dangerous. In 1912, the ship Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic Ocean and sank. Today, ships use radar and satellites to keep track of icebergs.

Glaciers and ice sheets hold most of the fresh water on our planet. As Earth grows warmer, many glaciers are melting and shrinking. Their meltwater flows into the oceans and makes sea levels rise, which is a serious concern for island nations like the Philippines.
